quiz.q: Natural theology is best defined as…
options: what can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided reason, apart from revelation
the study of nature as a form of worship
theology based on scripture and church authority
the scientific study of religious behaviour
quiz.explanation: Feser defines it this way in the Introduction. The contrast is with revealed theology, which begins from what God is taken to have disclosed; the other options describe nature religion and the empirical study of religion.

quiz.q: An argument is valid when…
options: all of its premises are true
if its premises were true, its conclusion would have to be true
it convinces most reasonable people
its conclusion is true
quiz.explanation: Validity is a matter of form alone. ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; so Fido is a reptile’ is valid with two false premises. Valid plus true premises is called sound.

quiz.q: Which of these is a conclusion indicator?
options: because
since
therefore
given that
quiz.explanation: ‘Therefore’ signals that what follows is being drawn from what came before. ‘Because’, ‘since’ and ‘given that’ all introduce premises.

quiz.q: Feser claims his five arguments are…
options: inferences to the best explanation
probabilistic design arguments
articles of faith supported by reason
demonstrations, whose conclusions follow necessarily from certain premises
quiz.explanation: He claims demonstration, not probability. This matters for how the arguments must be attacked: you need a false premise or an invalid step, not a rival hypothesis.

quiz.q: In Feser’s precise formulation, the principle of causality states that…
options: no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it
everything that exists has a cause
every event has a cause preceding it in time
everything has an explanation, in itself or in another
quiz.explanation: The second is the popular caricature Feser never asserts; the fourth is PSR, a distinct principle. PC concerns the actualization of potentials, which is why something with no potentials falls outside its scope.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a per accidens (linear) causal series?
options: a cup held by a desk held by a floor
a grandfather, a father, and a son
a lamp hanging from a chain from a ceiling fixture
layers of increasingly fundamental laws of nature
quiz.explanation: In a linear series, members keep their causal power once they have acted — the grandfather can be dead. The other three are hierarchical: each member’s power is derived at the moment it acts.

quiz.q: When Feser says a hierarchical series must have a ‘first’ member, ‘first’ means…
options: earliest in time
most powerful
having non-derivative causal power
occurring at the Big Bang
quiz.explanation: This is the most important terminological point in the book. A first cause has power built in rather than borrowed, which is why an infinitely long paintbrush handle still needs a painter.

quiz.q: Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides is that change does not involve something coming from nothing, because…
options: nothing really changes, only our perceptions do
change is an illusion produced by language
coming from nothing is actually possible
what comes to be was already present potentially, and a potential is not nothing
quiz.explanation: The coffee has a potential to grow cold and no potential to become chicken soup. That it has some potentials and lacks others shows potentiality is a real feature of it.

quiz.q: A substance, in Aristotle’s sense, is…
options: a thing that exists in its own right, such as this dog or this tree
a kind of material, such as bronze or water
any feature that can be predicated of something
the matter out of which a thing is made
quiz.explanation: Substance is contrasted with accident, which exists only in something else. The chemical sense of ‘substance’ as a kind of stuff is a different use of the word.

quiz.q: ‘The statue is made of bronze.’ Which of the four causes is being given?
options: formal cause
material cause
efficient cause
final cause
quiz.explanation: The material cause is what a thing is made of. The formal cause would be its statue-structure, the efficient cause the sculptor, the final cause what it is for.

quiz.q: Which distinction does the objection ‘but the universe might be infinitely old’ ignore?
options: validity versus soundness
essence versus existence
per se versus per accidens causal series
univocal versus analogical predication
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly grants a beginningless universe for the sake of argument. The arguments concern hierarchical series operating here and now, so the age of the universe is beside the point.

quiz.q: The three arguments chapter 4 gives for the real distinction between essence and existence appeal to…
options: scripture, tradition, and reason
observation, experiment, and calculation
Plato, Aristotle, and Plotinus
knowledge, contingency, and uniqueness
quiz.explanation: You can know an essence without knowing whether it is instantiated; contingent things would be necessary if existence were part of their essence; and there could be at most one thing whose essence is existence, while ordinary kinds come in multiples.

quiz.q: PSR differs from PC in that…
options: PSR entails everything has a sufficient reason, while PC does not entail everything has a cause
PSR concerns only physical objects
PC is about explanation and PSR about causation
PC was formulated by Leibniz and PSR by Aristotle
quiz.explanation: Chapter 5 draws this contrast carefully. A cause must be distinct from its effect, but a sufficient reason need not be, so something could in principle be self-explanatory.

quiz.q: Nominalism holds that…
options: universals exist as ideas in a divine intellect
only particular things exist; universals are merely names we apply
universals exist in a realm of their own
universals exist as concepts in human minds
quiz.explanation: From Latin nomen, ‘name’. The other options describe Scholastic realism, Platonic realism and conceptualism respectively.

quiz.q: In philosophy, to call something ‘simple’ is to say that it…
options: behaves predictably
is easy to grasp
has no parts of any kind
has only one function
quiz.explanation: Philosophical simplicity is non-compositeness — no physical or metaphysical parts. Feser holds God to be incomprehensible, so simplicity is very far from ease of understanding.

quiz.q: What distinguishes theistic personalism from classical theism?
options: theistic personalism denies that God is good
classical theism denies that God exists in any sense
classical theism denies that God has intellect or will
theistic personalism takes God to fall under a genus and so to be composite rather than simple
quiz.explanation: Feser is explicit that the difference is not about whether God is personal — most classical theists attribute intellect and will to God. It is about whether God falls under a genus.

quiz.q: ‘Good wine’ and ‘a good man’ illustrate which kind of predication?
options: analogical
univocal
equivocal
metaphorical
quiz.explanation: The senses are related but not identical — the middle option between univocal (same sense) and equivocal (unrelated senses). Feser insists analogical predication is literal, not metaphorical.

quiz.q: The fallacy of composition is committed when one…
options: attacks the person rather than the argument
infers that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole
assumes the conclusion in the premises
exempts a favoured case from a general rule
quiz.explanation: ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ The other options describe ad hominem, begging the question and special pleading. Note that not all part-to-whole reasoning is fallacious — every brick being red does make the wall red.

quiz.q: Which best describes the structure of each of Feser’s first five chapters?
options: history, then argument, then application
objections, then argument, then conclusion
informal Stage 1, informal Stage 2, formal statement, objections
formal statement, informal explanation, summary
quiz.explanation: Feser describes this pattern in the Introduction. Stage 1 argues that something fitting a key description exists; Stage 2 argues that it must have the divine attributes.

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘Even if there’s a first cause, why call it God?’ Where in the book is that question answered?
options: in the objections section at the end of each chapter
in the formal numbered statement
in the Introduction
in Stage 2 of the informal statement in each proof chapter
quiz.explanation: Stage 2 exists precisely to argue that whatever fits the Stage 1 description must have unity, immateriality, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience and perfect goodness. Skipping Stage 2 leaves you unable to answer the commonest objection.

quiz.q: The infinitely long paintbrush illustrates that…
options: adding members to a hierarchical series never supplies power none of them has
infinite series are logically impossible
causes must be simultaneous with their effects
the universe must have had a beginning
quiz.explanation: Length is not power. The point is specific to hierarchical series; Feser grants that linear series might in principle be infinite.

quiz.q: Which statement about a potential is accurate?
options: a potential is simply nothing at all
a potential is a real capacity limited by what the thing actually is
everything is potentially everything else
a potential can actualize itself given enough time
quiz.explanation: Coffee is potentially cold and not potentially chicken soup. That potentials discriminate is what shows they are real features of things, and a merely potential thing cannot act — only what is actual can.

quiz.q: The principle of proportionate causality says that what is in an effect must be in its total cause…
options: only formally
only by physical transfer
formally, virtually, or eminently
only if the cause is material
quiz.explanation: The $20 example: in my wallet (formally), in my bank account (virtually), or through access to a printing press (eminently). Feser and Aquinas both reject the ‘heirloom’ reading on which the same feature must be literally handed over.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a possible world in the philosophers’ sense?
options: a world with unicorns
a world with different laws of physics
a world in which Mars has three moons
a world in which some squares are round
quiz.explanation: Possible worlds are limited by logic, not by physics. A round square is self-contradictory, so there is no such world; the other three involve no contradiction.

quiz.q: Someone objects: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ The most accurate response is:
options: none of the arguments uses the premise ‘everything has a cause’, and each explains why its terminus could not in principle have one
God is an exception to the rule because he is God
the rule applies only to physical things
we cannot know the answer, which is why it is called faith
quiz.explanation: Feser opens chapter 7 with this objection. It attacks a straw man, and the arguments do more than exempt their terminus — they explain why what is purely actual, or simple, or whose essence is existence, could not have had a cause.

quiz.q: Scholastic realism differs from Platonic realism in holding that universals…
options: do not exist at all
exist as ideas in a divine intellect rather than in a separate third realm
exist only in human minds
are identical with the particular things that exhibit them
quiz.explanation: Chapter 3 keeps the reality of universals and rejects Plato’s free-floating realm, on the grounds that causally inert objects standing apart from everything would be disconnected and epistemically inaccessible.

quiz.q: Feser’s central case for PSR is that…
options: it has never been observed to fail
it is true by definition
denying it is self-undermining, since one could then have no reason to think one’s beliefs track truth
it follows directly from the principle of causality
quiz.explanation: Developing Pruss and Koons, chapter 5 argues by reductio: if PSR is false, we could have no grounds for thinking we hold any belief for good reasons — including any belief that PSR is false.

quiz.q: Which of these would a metaphysical part be?
options: a chair’s legs
the atoms of a molecule
a body’s organs
the distinction between a thing’s form and its matter
quiz.explanation: Metaphysical parts are really distinct principles within one thing, not separable components. Form and matter, essence and existence, act and potency, substance and accidents are the standard cases.

quiz.q: In classical theism, God’s omnipotence is best characterized as…
options: being that from which all causal power derives
the ability to do anything describable, including contradictions
having more power than any other being
the power to intervene in nature at will
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1 derives it in steps 33–37: all power is the ability to actualize potentials, every actualization traces to the purely actual actualizer, and to be that from which all power derives is what omnipotence means.

quiz.q: You read: ‘Since every event has a physical cause, and thought is an event, thought has a physical cause.’ The premises are…
options: the second and third statements
the first two statements, with the third as conclusion
all three statements
none — this is an explanation, not an argument
quiz.explanation: ‘Since’ flags the premises; the final clause is the conclusion. Identifying which statements are doing supporting work is the first move in reading any argument.

quiz.q: The shelf-with-no-explanation example in chapter 5 is directed against…
options: the ontological argument
the reality of universals
brute facts as terminators of explanation
the principle of proportionate causality
quiz.explanation: If the shelf stays aloft as a sheer brute fact, it has no tendency of its own to stay up and so cannot impart one to the book. The same applies to a bottom-level law of nature taken as brute.

quiz.q: Which of the five proofs is NOT a causal argument?
options: the Aristotelian proof
the Thomistic proof
the rationalist proof
the Augustinian proof
quiz.explanation: Feser notes in a footnote to chapter 7 that the ‘what caused God?’ objection is not even prima facie relevant to the Augustinian proof, because unlike the others it is not a causal argument.

quiz.q: A critic argues: ‘Power and knowledge are distinct in us, so they must be distinct in God, and divine simplicity fails.’ The unstated assumption is that…
options: the terms apply univocally to God and to creatures
God exists
knowledge is a species of power
God is composite
quiz.explanation: The inference goes through only if the words mean exactly the same in both cases. Classical theists apply them analogically, which is Feser’s reply to Plantinga in chapter 6.

quiz.q: The claim that a thing continues in existence on its own once it exists, needing no sustaining cause, is called…
options: occasionalism
existential inertia
divine concurrence
the principle of plenitude
quiz.explanation: It is the main rival to divine conservation, and the name is coined by analogy with Newtonian inertia — though that analogy concerns motion rather than existence.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches a thinker to the proof named for him?
options: Plotinus — the argument from universals to a divine intellect
Leibniz — the argument from change to an Unmoved Mover
Aquinas — the argument from essence and existence to subsistent existence itself
Augustine — the argument from composition to an absolutely simple cause
quiz.explanation: Aquinas presented this argument in On Being and Essence. Plotinus belongs with composition and the One, Augustine with universals and the divine intellect, Leibniz with PSR and the necessary being.

quiz.q: A skeptic says: ‘Science will eventually explain everything you’re appealing to.’ The most accurate reply is:
options: science has already reached its limits
no scientific result could bear on these arguments, since science is unreliable
these arguments concern features anything whatever must have, not phenomena awaiting a mechanism
the gaps in current science are permanent
quiz.explanation: This is what distinguishes the arguments from god-of-the-gaps reasoning. A complete physics would describe how things within the world behave and would not address why anything exists or what sustains it.

quiz.q: The ‘one god further’ objection fails, on Feser’s account, because…
options: atheists have not examined every religion
Zeus might exist after all
polytheism is more coherent than monotheism
it treats the God of classical theism as a being within the universe, like Zeus, rather than the source of existence itself
quiz.explanation: Chapter 7 argues the objection rests on a category confusion. Rejecting a powerful being inside the world is a different kind of act from rejecting that in virtue of which anything exists.

quiz.q: What is a hidden premise?
options: an assumption an argument needs but does not state
a premise deliberately concealed to deceive
a conclusion drawn earlier in the text
a premise that is false
quiz.explanation: ‘He’s a politician, so he’s lying’ hides the premise that all politicians lie. Digging out the unstated assumption is usually where an argument’s real weakness turns up.

quiz.q: According to the principle agere sequitur esse…
options: every effect must resemble its cause
a thing’s activities follow from and cannot exceed its nature
action requires an external mover
being follows from action
quiz.explanation: Latin for ‘action follows being’. A stone cannot take in nutrients because that would exceed the nature of a stone; it is the formal-causal counterpart of the principle of proportionate causality.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order for working through a module of this course?
options: read the chapter, then prepare, then watch the video
watch the video, then read the chapter, then skip the practice
prepare with the module, watch the video, read the chapter, return to practise
read the chapter twice, then take the quiz
quiz.explanation: Preparation removes the vocabulary obstacle, the video orients you, the chapter supplies the argument, and returning for practice is what turns reading into understanding.

quiz.q: ‘Every part of this machine is lightweight, so the machine is lightweight.’ This is…
options: a fallacy of composition
begging the question
a straw man
an ad hominem
quiz.explanation: It moves from a property of the parts to the whole where that inference does not hold. Weight aggregates; colour does not, which is why ‘every brick is red, so the wall is red’ is fine.

quiz.q: Which best captures why a composite thing cannot account for the union of its own parts?
options: because parts always predate wholes
because to do the uniting it would have to exist already, and its existing presupposes the union
because composites have no causal powers
because the parts might be infinitely divisible
quiz.explanation: That would be an explanatory circle. Something distinct from the composite must account for its parts being united, which is the engine of chapter 2’s argument.

quiz.q: In classical theism, God’s eternity means…
options: endless duration through time
a very long lifespan
existence outside time altogether
existence from the Big Bang onward
quiz.explanation: Step 22 of chapter 1 reasons that existing in time would involve change, which pure actuality excludes. Eternity here is timelessness, not sempiternity.

quiz.q: The two — and only two — honest ways to attack a deductive argument are to…
options: question the author’s motives or point to expert disagreement
show the conclusion is unpopular or that it has bad consequences
demand more evidence or propose a rival hypothesis
show that a premise is false or that an inference does not follow
quiz.explanation: Everything else leaves the argument untouched. Proposing a rival hypothesis is appropriate against an inference to the best explanation, which is precisely what Feser claims his proofs are not.

quiz.q: ‘Mind-independent’, in the debate about universals, means independent of…
options: human minds
all minds whatsoever
physical reality
language
quiz.explanation: This is why Scholastic realism is not self-contradictory: universals can be independent of our minds while existing as ideas in a divine intellect.

quiz.q: Which question is Feser asking when he asks what causes the coffee to exist?
options: who poured it and when
what is actualizing its potential for existence at this very moment
what will eventually destroy it
what its chemical composition is
quiz.explanation: He explicitly sets aside how it got here and how it might go out of existence. The question is what keeps it in existence at any instant at which it exists.

quiz.q: Special pleading would be committed if one…
options: gave a principled reason why a case falls outside a rule
applied a rule consistently to all cases
exempted a favoured case from a general rule without a principled reason
refused to state one’s rule at all
quiz.explanation: Feser’s defence against this charge is that the arguments give the principled reason: things need causes because of a specific feature — potentiality, composition, contingency — that the terminus lacks.

quiz.q: A reader complains that she cannot picture a timeless, partless being and concludes the idea is nonsense. The best reply is:
options: imagination is the test of meaning, so the complaint stands
the idea is indeed meaningless but useful
she should try harder to visualize it
imaginability is not the test of intelligibility — one cannot picture the number seventeen either, yet reasons about it perfectly well
quiz.explanation: The intellect grasps what the imagination cannot supply a picture for; that is what distinguishes them. Chapter 6’s doctrine of divine incomprehensibility concedes that God is not exhaustively graspable while insisting that true things can be known of him.

shortAnswer.q: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a sound one, and give an example of an argument that is valid but not sound.
shortAnswer.model:
Validity concerns form alone: an argument is valid when, if its premises were true, its conclusion would have to be true. Soundness adds a further requirement — that the premises actually are true. So every sound argument is valid, but not every valid argument is sound.

An example: ‘All cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; therefore Fido is a reptile.’ The reasoning is impeccable — given those premises, the conclusion follows necessarily — but both premises are false, so the argument establishes nothing.

The practical payoff is that it fixes the only two honest ways to attack a deductive argument: show that an inference does not follow, or show that a premise is false. Disliking the conclusion, doubting the author, or noting that clever people disagree leaves the argument untouched.
rubric: States that validity is about form: if the premises were true the conclusion would have to be true
States that soundness = validity plus actually true premises
Gives a correct example of a valid argument with a false premise
Notes that every sound argument is valid but not conversely
Draws the consequence for how deductive arguments must be attacked

shortAnswer.q: Explain the difference between a linear (per accidens) and a hierarchical (per se) causal series, with one example of each, and say why only one of them must have a first member.
shortAnswer.model:
A linear series runs backward through time and its members keep their causal power once they have acted. Your grandfather caused your father, who caused you; your grandfather can be long dead and the chain still stands. Feser grants for the sake of argument that such a series might be infinite.

A hierarchical series is different: every member except the first has its causal power only derivatively, receiving it at the moment it acts. The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it, the desk only because the floor holds the desk, the floor only because the foundation. Remove the floor and everything above it falls at once. The intermediates are like instruments — a brush does not paint, the painter paints with it.

Only the hierarchical kind must have a first member, because all its members are borrowers, and adding borrowers never produces a lender. A paintbrush cannot move itself and would not move itself if its handle were infinitely long. Note that ‘first’ here means non-derivative — having the power built in — not earliest in time.

One nuance: simultaneity is a teaching aid, not the definition. What makes a series hierarchical is the derivative character of the later members, not their sharing a moment on the clock.
rubric: Defines linear series and notes members retain their own power
Defines hierarchical series in terms of derivative or instrumental power
Gives a correct example of each
Explains why only the hierarchical kind needs a first member, using length-is-not-power reasoning
States explicitly that ‘first’ means non-derivative, not earliest
Bonus: notes that simultaneity is illustrative rather than definitional

shortAnswer.q: State the principle of causality in Feser’s precise form and explain why the difference from ‘everything has a cause’ matters.
shortAnswer.model:
Feser’s formulation is: no potential can be actualized unless something already actual actualizes it. It is step 4 of chapter 1’s formal argument.

The support is conceptual rather than merely empirical. A merely potential F cannot do anything, precisely because it is merely potential; acting is the prerogative of the actual. Potential coldness chills nothing; actual coldness does.

The difference from ‘everything has a cause’ matters enormously. If the arguments used the popular premise, then their conclusion would be an arbitrary exception and the objection ‘who made God?’ would be devastating. But they do not use it. PC applies to potentials being actualized, so something with no potentials is not exempted — the principle simply has nothing to say about it.

And the arguments go further than declining to apply the rule: they explain why the terminus could not in principle have a cause. Things need causes because they are mixtures of act and potency, or have parts to be united, or have an essence distinct from their existence, or are contingent. What is purely actual has no potentials to be actualized at all.
rubric: States PC accurately in terms of potentials and something already actual
Explains the support: only what is actual can act
Contrasts it explicitly with ‘everything has a cause’
Explains why the difference defuses the ‘who made God?’ objection
Notes that the arguments explain why the terminus could not have a cause, not merely that it does not need one

shortAnswer.q: What is natural theology, and how does it differ both from revealed theology and from empirical science?
shortAnswer.model:
Natural theology is the attempt to establish what can be known about God’s existence and nature by unaided human reason, apart from divine revelation. Feser defines it this way in the Introduction, and the whole book is an exercise in it.

It differs from revealed theology in its starting points. Revealed theology reasons from what God is taken to have disclosed — scripture, tradition, prophecy. Natural theology uses no such premise. That is why you will not find an appeal to scripture or church authority anywhere in the five proofs.

It differs from empirical science in the kind of question it asks. Science investigates how things within the world behave: what mechanisms operate, under what laws, in what order. Natural theology asks why there is anything at all, and what sustains anything in being from moment to moment. No measurement can address those questions, since any measurement presupposes something there to measure.

That second difference is also why these arguments are not god-of-the-gaps reasoning. A gaps argument points to something science has not yet explained; these arguments point to features anything whatever must have.
rubric: Defines natural theology as knowledge of God by unaided reason apart from revelation
Contrasts it with revealed theology by its starting premises
Contrasts it with science by the kind of question asked
Notes that no premise in the book is drawn from scripture or authority
Connects the science contrast to why the arguments are not god-of-the-gaps

shortAnswer.q: Explain actuality and potentiality using two examples, and say why Feser insists that a potential is not the same as nothing.
shortAnswer.model:
Actuality is the way a thing really is at a given moment; potentiality is a real capacity it has but is not exercising. Hot coffee is actually hot and liquid; it is potentially cold, potentially spilled, potentially a stain on the carpet. Water in a freezer is actually liquid and potentially solid.

A potential is not nothing, and the reason is that potentials discriminate. The coffee has a potential to grow cold; it has no potential to become chicken soup, to fuel a gasoline engine, or to turn into a live chicken. If potentiality were sheer nothingness, there would be nothing to distinguish the potentials a thing has from those it lacks.

This is Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides, who argued that change is impossible because the new state was nothing beforehand and something afterward, and nothing comes from nothing. Change is not something from nothing; it is the actualization of an already-real capacity.

Feser also answers the charge that potentiality is an empty concept, made by Cottingham in chapter 6. His reply is that explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, but minimally informative is not uninformative — a concept that rules things out is not empty.
rubric: Defines actuality and potentiality clearly
Gives at least two concrete examples
Argues that potentials are real because they discriminate — some are had, others not
Connects this to Parmenides’ problem and Aristotle’s solution
Addresses or anticipates the objection that potentiality explains nothing

shortAnswer.q: What is a real distinction, how does it differ from a distinction of reason, and what are the three arguments chapter 4 gives that essence and existence are really distinct?
shortAnswer.model:
A real distinction holds in mind-independent reality; a distinction of reason reflects only our way of thinking or speaking. ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ pick out exactly the same reality, so that distinction is one of reason. A real distinction may be between two things, or between two really distinct principles within one thing — which is the case with essence and existence.

The three arguments are these. First, from knowledge: describe lions, pterodactyls and unicorns fully to someone who has never heard of them, and he still cannot say which exists. Since both essence and existence belong to a thing’s objective reality, if they were not distinct, grasping the first would deliver the second. Second, from contingency: if a lion’s existence were included in its essence, it would exist by its very nature and so could not fail to exist. Since lions are contingent, the distinction is real. Third, from uniqueness: there could be at most one thing whose essence just is existence, since differentiating two such things would make each ‘existence itself plus something’. But ordinary kinds come in multiples, so in each of them essence and existence are distinct.

The payoff is that anything in which they are really distinct needs something conjoining them at every moment it exists — which sets a hierarchical series running toward subsistent existence itself.
rubric: Defines real distinction and contrasts it with distinction of reason with an example
Gives the argument from knowledge (lions, pterodactyls, unicorns)
Gives the argument from contingency
Gives the argument from uniqueness
States the consequence: such things need a cause conjoining essence and existence at every moment

shortAnswer.q: State the principle of sufficient reason and explain Feser’s main argument for it.
shortAnswer.model:
PSR says that everything has an explanation of why it exists and why it has the attributes it has — either in something else or in itself. Two Thomistic formulations Feser quotes are that everything which is has a sufficient reason for existing, and that everything is intelligible.

He offers an inductive case: we do in fact find explanations when we look, and even when we do not, we usually have reason to think there is one we lack access to. A world where PSR failed should be full of constantly occurring inexplicable events, and the success of science and common sense would be miraculous.

But he holds PSR is more certain than any empirical hypothesis and argues for it indirectly, by reductio. Developing Pruss and Koons: if PSR is false, there might be no connection whatever between our perceptions and the world, and no basis for calling such a disconnect improbable. Worse, we could have no reason to think we hold any belief because of good reasons rather than for no reason at all, while it falsely seemed otherwise. Since that applies to any grounds for doubting PSR, rejecting PSR is self-undermining.

He also argues that explanations terminating in brute facts are illusory: a shelf with no tendency of its own to stay aloft cannot impart such a tendency to the book on it.
rubric: States PSR accurately, including the in-itself-or-in-another disjunction
Gives the inductive support
Gives the reductio: denying PSR is self-undermining
Explains why that undercuts any argument against PSR too
Mentions the case against brute facts as explanation-terminators

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish realism, nominalism and conceptualism about universals, and explain why chapter 3 rejects two of the three.
shortAnswer.model:
Realism holds that universals — the general patterns many things share, like redness or triangularity — are real and exist independently of human minds. Nominalism holds that only particular things exist and that ‘redness’ is merely a name we apply to a group of individuals. Conceptualism holds that universals exist, but only as concepts in human minds.

Chapter 3 rejects nominalism and conceptualism on the same underlying ground: both make abstract truths depend on us. But mathematical and logical truths hold whether or not any human being thinks them. Seven was prime before there were humans and would remain so if humanity vanished. Erase every instance of ‘Snow is white’ and of ‘Schnee ist weiss’ in every language, and the proposition they expressed is still true. Names and concepts are things we make; these truths are not.

Feser also rejects Plato’s version of realism, which places universals in a third realm apart from all minds and physical things. The objection is that such objects would be causally inert and disconnected, leaving it mysterious how they relate to the world and how we could know them. The alternative, Scholastic realism, keeps universals mind-independent with respect to our minds while grounding them in a divine intellect.
rubric: Defines all three positions accurately
Gives the shared objection to nominalism and conceptualism: abstract truths do not depend on us
Supports it with an example such as mathematical truth or the proposition/sentence distinction
Explains the separate objection to Platonic realism
States the Scholastic realist alternative and notes that ‘mind-independent’ means independent of human minds

shortAnswer.q: What does it mean to say that something is ‘simple’ in the philosophical sense, and why does chapter 2 argue that the ultimate cause of things must be simple?
shortAnswer.model:
Simplicity in this sense means having no parts whatsoever — not that the thing is easy to understand. And ‘parts’ is meant broadly. Besides physical parts, it includes metaphysical parts: form and matter, essence and existence, substance and accidents, actuality and potentiality, genus and specific difference.

The argument runs as follows. Anything composite depends on its parts existing and being united. This is not primarily a point about assembly over time — your organs were never made separately and bolted together, and a chair that had always existed would still depend at every moment on its parts. The composite itself cannot be what unites its parts, since it exists only given that union, which would be an explanatory circle. So something distinct from it must account for the union.

That generates a hierarchical series, which must terminate in something with no parts to be united in the first place. Hence an absolutely simple cause — what Plotinus called the One.

One important consequence: if God is simple, his power, knowledge and goodness are not three components bolted together but one reality grasped under several concepts. That is coherent only because our language about God is analogical rather than univocal.
rubric: Defines simplicity as having no parts and distinguishes it from ease of understanding
Lists metaphysical as well as physical parts
Gives the dependence argument and the explanatory-circle point
Explains that the regress terminates in something with no parts at all
Notes the consequence for the divine attributes and its connection to analogy

shortAnswer.q: Contrast classical theism with theistic personalism, and explain why the difference matters for evaluating objections to theism.
shortAnswer.model:
Classical theism holds that God is pure actuality — absolutely simple, immutable, eternal, necessary, omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good — and is not one being among others but the source of the existence of everything else. Theistic personalism, also called neo-theism, treats God as the unique member of a species falling under the genus person, alongside human beings and angels, differing from them by lacking their limitations in power, knowledge and goodness.

It is essential to get the disagreement right. It is not that classical theists deny God is personal — most attribute intellect and will to him and regard him as personal. The dispute is whether God falls under a genus, and so is composite rather than simple. Some theistic personalists go further: process theologians such as Hartshorne deny divine immutability, but to be changeable is to have potentials as well as actualities, and so to be composite.

The difference matters because most popular objections target the personalist picture. ‘Who designed the designer?’, ‘God is an extra entity that Ockham’s razor shaves off’, and ‘you’re an atheist about every god but one’ all presuppose that God is one item in the world’s inventory, subject to the same questions as the others. Against classical theism they do not land, because the conclusion of the arguments is not another instance of existence but the source of it.
rubric: Characterizes classical theism by pure actuality and simplicity
Characterizes theistic personalism by God falling under a genus
States explicitly that the difference is not about whether God is personal
Gives at least two objections that target the personalist picture
Explains why those objections miss classical theism

shortAnswer.q: Explain univocal, equivocal and analogical predication with an example of each, and say why the distinction matters for talk about God.
shortAnswer.model:
Univocal predication uses a word in exactly the same sense in both cases: ‘Fido is a dog’ and ‘Rover is a dog’. Equivocal predication uses it in wholly unrelated senses that happen to share a spelling: the bat that flew around the attic and the bat you swung at it. Analogical predication is the middle case — related but not identical senses: ‘this wine is good’ and ‘George is a good man’.

Classical theists hold that terms applied to God are used analogically. This is not a fudge but the only remaining option once the alternatives are run out. If God-talk were univocal, God’s goodness would be the same kind of thing as human goodness — an accident of a composite, limited being — and the arguments show that such a thing needs a cause. If it were equivocal, theology would be noise and the conclusions of the proofs could not even be stated.

Two points are easy to get wrong. First, analogical predication is literal. ‘God is good’ is a true, literal claim; ‘God is a rock’ is metaphor. Feser objects specifically to the characterization of Aquinas’ view as holding that God-talk is analogical rather than literal. Second, analogy is not confined to theology — we use ‘real’ analogically of a stone and of the stone’s colour without noticing.

It matters because many objections to classical theism run on an unnoticed assumption of univocity, including Plantinga’s argument that God’s power and knowledge must be distinct because ours are.
rubric: Defines all three with a correct example of each
States that God-talk is analogical on the classical view
Explains why both extremes fail
Insists that analogical is literal, not metaphorical
Shows how the distinction defuses at least one concrete objection

shortAnswer.q: Name four fallacies the book repeatedly discusses and give an everyday example of each.
shortAnswer.model:
**Fallacy of composition** — inferring that what is true of the parts must be true of the whole. ‘Every brick is light, so the wall is light.’ Note that this is not always fallacious: every brick being red does make the wall red, so whether the inference works depends on the property.

**Begging the question** — assuming in the premises what the argument is supposed to establish. ‘This book is reliable because it says so, and what it says is true because the book is reliable.’ The argument cannot move anyone not already persuaded.

**Straw man** — refuting a weakened version of a position instead of the one actually held. Attacking ‘everything has a cause, except God’ when no proponent of these arguments holds it. Feser argues in chapter 7 that the textbook ‘basic cosmological argument’ is exactly this, with a long pedigree.

**Special pleading** — exempting a favoured case from a general rule without a principled reason. ‘Everything needs a cause, except God, because he’s God.’ Feser’s defence is that the arguments supply the principled reason: things need causes because of a feature — potentiality, composition, contingency — that the terminus lacks.

A fifth worth knowing is **god of the gaps**: invoking God to fill a hole in current science, so that the explanation dies when the hole is filled.
rubric: Names at least four of composition, begging the question, straw man, special pleading, god of the gaps, ad hominem
Gives a correct everyday example of each named
Explains why each pattern fails
Connects at least two to how they arise in debates about these arguments
Bonus: notes that part-to-whole reasoning is not always fallacious

shortAnswer.q: A friend says: ‘Even if your argument works, you’ve only got some abstract first cause. Why call that God?’ How should you answer, and where does the book handle it?
shortAnswer.model:
This is the strongest of the beginner-level objections and deserves to be taken seriously rather than brushed aside. The book handles it in Stage 2 of the informal statement in each of the first five chapters — which is exactly why skipping Stage 2 leaves readers unable to answer the objection they will meet most often.

The strategy is to show that anything fitting the Stage 1 description must, by the same metaphysics, have further features. If it were material it would have unactualized potentials, so it is immaterial. If it were in time it would change, so it is eternal. There could not be two, since differentiating them would make each ‘pure actuality plus something’, so it is unique. All causal power derives from it, which is what omnipotence means. The patterns of everything it causes must be present in it somehow, and in a purely actual immaterial cause they can only be present in the manner of intellect — hence omniscience. To fall short of goodness is to fail to actualize something, and there is no such failure, hence perfect goodness.

A rival candidate such as a quantum field fails because it is one physical thing among others, with states, parts and potentials — a candidate for a member of the series, not its terminus.

Be honest about the limits, though. Natural theology does not deliver any particular revealed religion, and Feser says so in the Introduction: he thinks the real debate begins where natural theology leaves off.
rubric: Identifies Stage 2 of each proof chapter as where this is answered
Describes the general strategy: the same metaphysics yields the further attributes
Gives at least three specific derivations
Explains why a physical candidate such as a quantum field fails
Acknowledges honestly what natural theology does not deliver

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser insist his proofs are demonstrations rather than probabilistic arguments, and what difference does that make to how they should be criticized?
shortAnswer.model:
A demonstration is a valid deductive argument from premises that are certain; its conclusion follows necessarily. An inference to the best explanation, by contrast, accepts the hypothesis that accounts for the evidence better than its rivals, and yields a conclusion that is probable and defeasible.

Feser claims demonstration, and the claim is not modest: in the Introduction he says a long line of thinkers held that God’s existence can be rationally demonstrated by purely philosophical arguments, and that the aim of his book is to show they were right.

The difference matters for criticism. Against a best-explanation argument, it is fair to say ‘some other hypothesis might do better’, ‘science may yet find a natural cause’, or ‘this is a god-of-the-gaps move’. Against a purported demonstration these replies are beside the point, because the argument does not rest on being the best available account of some phenomenon. There are only two ways in: show that a premise is false, or show that an inference does not follow.

This is also why the objection sections matter so much. They are where Feser states the best attempts to do exactly those two things, and they are the fastest route to finding out whether the arguments survive.
rubric: Defines demonstration and contrasts it with inference to the best explanation
Notes that Feser explicitly claims the stronger status
Explains that rival-hypothesis and gaps objections are appropriate only to the weaker kind
States the two legitimate lines of attack
Connects this to the role of the objection sections

shortAnswer.q: Describe the structure of each of Feser’s first five chapters and give practical advice for reading a fifty-step formal argument without panic.
shortAnswer.model:
Each of the first five chapters has four parts. First, an informal statement in Stage 1, arguing discursively that something fitting a key description exists. Second, an informal Stage 2, arguing that anything fitting that description must have the divine attributes. Third, a formal statement setting the reasoning out as explicit numbered steps. Fourth, objections — which Feser notes are in some cases the most technical material in the chapter.

For the numbered argument, four habits help. First, remember it is a recap: it introduces no material the informal pages have not already supplied, so a baffling step is explained earlier. Second, find the joints — in chapter 1, steps 1–5 establish change and the principle of causality, 6–14 run the hierarchical-series argument to a purely actual actualizer, 15–18 establish uniqueness, and 19–47 derive the attributes. Read four blocks, not fifty steps. Third, label every step as premise, inference or conclusion; steps beginning ‘So’ are inferences and need only a valid link, so the weight is on the premises. Fourth, attack rather than absorb: after each block, ask which single step you would challenge first.

It also helps to know what can wait. Feser starts at the shallow end and ends in the deep end by design, so difficulty near the end of a chapter is the structure working, not a personal failure. The science-based objections in chapter 1 can be skimmed on a first read and returned to.
rubric: Names all four parts of a proof chapter in order
Explains what Stage 1 and Stage 2 each secure
Gives at least three concrete reading tactics for the formal argument
Notes that the formal statement is a recap of the informal pages
Mentions that difficulty increases by design and what can be deferred

shortAnswer.q: Someone objects that these arguments are god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Explain why Feser denies this, and what would make an argument genuinely of that kind.
shortAnswer.model:
A god-of-the-gaps argument points to something current science has not explained and proposes God as the filler. Its weakness is structural: the explanation dies as soon as the gap closes, so the position retreats with every advance.

Feser denies that his arguments have this form, and addresses the charge in chapter 7 around page 271. The reason is that they do not rest on any gap in scientific knowledge. They begin from features that anything whatever must have: that it changes, that it has parts, that its essence is not its existence, that it is contingent. No account of mechanism could address these, because any mechanism you propose has the very same features and so raises the same question.

This is also why the arguments are indifferent to cosmology. Feser grants a beginningless universe or multiverse for the sake of argument. An argument that needed the universe to have had a beginning would indeed be hostage to future physics; his is not.

The practical lesson for anyone defending the arguments is to avoid citing scientific mysteries — consciousness, fine-tuning, the origin of life — as support. Doing so converts a demonstration into precisely the gaps argument the objector was expecting.
rubric: Defines god-of-the-gaps reasoning and states why it is weak
Explains that the arguments start from universal features rather than unexplained phenomena
Notes that any proposed mechanism has the same features
Connects this to Feser’s granting of a beginningless universe
Draws the practical lesson about not citing scientific mysteries

shortAnswer.q: Explain the principle of proportionate causality using the $20 example, and say how Feser answers the charge that it is refuted by counterexamples like sponge cake.
shortAnswer.model:
PPC says that whatever is in an effect must in some way be in its total cause — a cause cannot give what it does not have. The ‘in some way’ is crucial, and the $20 example unpacks it. If I give you $20, I might have the bill in my wallet and hand it over: what is in the effect was in the cause **formally**. Or I might have no cash but $20 in the bank and wire it: it was in the total cause — me plus my account — **virtually**, as a power to obtain it. Or I might have access to a Federal Reserve printing press and have a bill run off: it was there **eminently**, as a more fundamental power to make such bills.

Cottingham objects that a sponge cake has sponginess that was in none of its ingredients, and that helium has properties hydrogen lacked. Feser gives three replies. First, the objection restricts PPC to material factors, when the principle concerns the *total* cause — which is itself a straw man. Second, the ‘heirloom’ reading, on which the same feature must literally be handed over, is one defenders of PPC explicitly reject; as one Thomist puts it, a boy need not have a black eye to give one. Third, Cottingham grants that the sponginess emerges from the chemical changes but complains that saying it was potentially present makes PPC trivial. Feser replies that explanations in terms of potentiality may be minimally informative, but minimally informative is not trivial or uninformative.

He adds that naturalist philosophers use PPC implicitly — Churchland argues that purely material beginnings plus purely material processes yield a purely material result, which assumes exactly this principle.
rubric: States PPC accurately including the ‘total cause’ qualification
Explains formally, virtually and eminently with the $20 example
States Cottingham’s counterexample fairly
Gives at least two of Feser’s replies, including the rejection of the heirloom reading
Bonus: notes that naturalist philosophers use the principle implicitly

shortAnswer.q: A friend says: ‘Philosophers have argued about this for 2,500 years without agreement, so nobody has a proof.’ Evaluate this reasoning.
shortAnswer.model:
The premise is true and the inference does not follow.

First, the argument proves too much. Informed, intelligent people still disagree about whether mathematical objects exist, whether determinism is true, and how to interpret quantum mechanics. Nobody concludes that these questions have no answers or that the arguments about them are worthless.

Second, and more fundamentally, an argument’s force is not settled by a head-count. A demonstration is refuted by a false premise or an invalid step, not by a survey of opinion. Feser takes this up at the close of chapter 7 (around page 307), arguing that a conclusion’s being controversial does not entail that the argument for it fails as a demonstration. If it did, a valid proof would cease to be one the moment someone clever refused to accept it.

Third, the picture of philosophy as making no progress is inaccurate. It progresses by ruling out positions, sharpening distinctions and exposing bad arguments rather than by producing unanimity — and much of chapter 7 is exactly that kind of work.

What the objection does get right is that persistent expert disagreement is a reason for intellectual humility about one’s own confidence. That is a fair conclusion; ‘therefore nobody has a proof’ is not.
rubric: Identifies that the inference from disagreement to failure does not follow
Gives a parallel case where we do not draw that conclusion
States that demonstrations are refuted by premises and inferences, not head-counts
Notes where Feser addresses this (end of chapter 7)
Concedes what is legitimate in the objection
